_comment: How it works: game-mechanic tutorial cards (scripts/how_it_works.gd). Very simple language. lines: what to know, one idea each. remember: the one thing to take away. check: one tap-to-answer question, never graded. missions: shown in these missions' briefs. triggers: items or zones whose first placement shows the card once.

cards.title: Landing safely
lines: A lander can't hit an exact spot. It comes down somewhere inside an oval called the landing ellipse.
Its rocket engine blasts rocks and dust in every direction as it lands.
So your base must sit outside the blast zone, but close enough to walk to the cargo.
cards.remember: Land on flat, clear ground, and keep the base out of the blast zone.

check.question: Why can't you build right next to the landing target?
options: The engine blast would damage it

cards.title: Testing your design
lines: Press T to run a Test. It fast-forwards your base through the whole mission in a few seconds.
The report shows what passed, what failed, and why, with graphs.
Every Test is saved as a version, so you can see what each change did.
Engineers do this too: design, test, improve, and test again.
cards.remember: Failing a Test is normal. Read why, change one thing, and test again.

check.question: Your Test fails. What's the best next step?
options: Read the reason, change something, test again

cards.title: Power, day and night
lines: Solar arrays make power only while the sun is up. At night they make none.
Batteries store spare power in the day and give it back at night.
If the batteries run flat, the base switches things off to save power: labs and drills first, then lights, then heating. Life support goes last.
A reactor makes the same power day and night, whatever the weather.
cards.remember: Make more power than you use in the day, and store enough to last the night.

check.question: It's midnight. Where does the base's power come from?

cards.title: Water from ice
lines: Mars has ice buried under the ground. An ice extractor drills it out and melts it into water.
Pale blue ground has more ice, so drills make more water there. GAR-Y can survey to find it.
Drills need power to work, including at night.
Later, a water reclaimer cleans used water so it can be used again.
cards.remember: Put drills on rich ice and keep them powered.

check.question: Where should you put an ice extractor?
options: On pale blue ground, where the ice is richest
As far from the base as possible

cards.title: Giving GAR-Y orders
lines: GAR-Y is your survey rover. Hold G near it to open its orders, move the mouse to one and let go.
Outside: Find ice (it surveys the likely zone itself and reports the best spot), Survey there, Core sample, Come here, Stay, Go home.
Inside: Fetch, Patrol, Come here, Stay, Go home.
It never goes through an airlock on its own. Press E on it so it follows you through.
cards.remember: Hold G and point. GAR-Y does the scouting so you don't have to.

check.question: How do you get GAR-Y outside?
options: Press E on it so it follows you through the airlock
Order it to open the airlock

cards.title: Keeping warm
lines: Mars is freezing, so heat leaks out of the habitat all the time. Windows and outside walls leak the most.
A spot heater only warms its own room and the rooms right next to it.
A thermal control unit is like central heating. It is ducted to every room, and gives about 3 times more heat for the same power.
A room that doesn't get enough heat becomes a cold spot.
cards.remember: One thermal control unit warms the whole base. Spot heaters are for small bases, far rooms, or backup.

check.question: Which one warms every room in the base?

cards.title: Air to breathe
lines: Every person breathes in oxygen and breathes out carbon dioxide (CO₂).
An oxygen generator makes oxygen by splitting water. It needs power and water.
An air recycler takes the CO₂ out of the air. Too much CO₂ gives people headaches, and then it's dangerous.
Oxygen reserve tanks top the air up if it starts to run low.
cards.remember: Oxygen in, CO₂ out: you need both machines, and both need power.

check.question: Which machine removes the CO₂ people breathe out?

cards.title: Looking after the crew
lines: Each crew member needs a bunk, air, water, food and warmth.
If any of those go wrong, crew health starts to fall. Fix it, and they slowly recover.
No bunk means no room: crew without one wait on the lander.
The habitat warns you early. Listen for its voice and check the alerts.
cards.remember: Bunk, air, water, food, warmth: keep all five safe for every crew member.

check.question: Crew health is falling. What should you check first?
options: The alerts: they say what's wrong

cards.title: Food
lines: The crew each eat about 1.8 kg of food a sol.
Food brought from Earth runs out one day, and the next delivery is a long way off.
Grow trays in Hydroponics grow food. They need power, water and light.
The more food you grow, the longer the base can last on its own.
cards.remember: Bring food to start, then grow more of it yourself.

cards.title: Dust storms
lines: A dust storm blocks the sun for days, so solar arrays make much less power.
Orbiters spot storms coming, so you get a warning first. Charge the batteries!
A reactor isn't affected: it makes the same power in any weather.
When power runs short, life support keeps going longest.
cards.remember: Before a storm: full batteries. For long storms: a reactor.

check.question: Which power source keeps working in a dust storm?

cards.title: Research
lines: Research is why the crew came to Mars.
A Science Lab with a workbench lets the crew do experiments every sol.
Equipment in the lab adds more research, if it has power.
GAR-Y can bring a core sample from outside for a boost.
cards.remember: A powered lab with a workbench, and the research adds up every sol.

check.question: What does the crew need to start research?
options: A Science Lab with a workbench

cards.title: Radiation and the shelter
lines: Mars has no magnetic field and thin air, so radiation from the Sun reaches the ground.
Sometimes the Sun throws out a burst of radiation called a solar particle event. You get about half an hour's warning.
The crew hide in a storm shelter: a small room with lots of shielding round it.
Shield points: the hull gives 5. Regolith walls and water walls add more, shared over the room's floor. Aim for 20.
cards.remember: A small room with lots of shielding makes a safe shelter.

check.question: Why is a small shelter easier to make safe?
options: The same shielding is shared over less floor
Radiation can't fit in small rooms

cards.title: Staying fit, getting better
lines: Mars gravity is only 38% of Earth's. Without exercise, bones and muscles slowly get weaker.
Each powered exercise station keeps about 3 crew fit. Six crew need two.
If someone gets hurt, they get better in a Medical Bay with an exam cot and a medical cabinet.
Tired or hurt crew work slower, so less research and food gets done.
cards.remember: Exercise every sol, and keep a Medical Bay ready.

check.question: How many exercise stations do six crew need?

cards.title: Feeling okay
lines: Living far from home in a small base is hard. Wellbeing shows how the crew are feeling.
It depends on six needs: sleep, space, meals together, a bit of home, meaningful work and contact with Earth.
The Crew screen in Mission Control shows which needs are missing, and what would fix them.
Wellbeing changes slowly, over a few sols, so fix problems early.
cards.remember: Look after all six needs, not just the numbers.

cards.title: Breaches and hatches
lines: A tiny space rock can punch a hole in the hull. Air starts rushing out.
Hatches (interior doors) seal by themselves. Rooms joined without a hatch, like an open corridor end, lose their air together.
Air pressure shows how much of the habitat still holds its air.
A patch kit seals the hole. Then an air reserve rack refills the empty rooms.
cards.remember: Build in sections: hatches keep a breach small.

check.question: Why put a hatch at the end of a corridor?
options: So a breach only empties one small section

cards.title: Breakdowns and spares
lines: Machines wear out. Far from Earth, the crew have to fix them.
Each repair uses a spare part, and the Engineer is fastest.
Redundancy means having two of everything that keeps people alive. If one breaks, the other carries on.
A running regolith printer slowly makes more spares.
cards.remember: Two of everything life-critical, and spares to fix them.

check.question: An air recycler breaks. What keeps the crew safe until it's fixed?
